title: What am I taking for granted?
prompt: Think of something you said or wrote recently that you were sure about. Look for the assumptions underneath it.
steps: Write the statement in one sentence.
List two or three things that would have to be true for the statement to hold.
Mark the one you have the least evidence for.
Write down one small way to find out whether it is true.

title: Fact or interpretation?
prompt: Pick a situation that bothered you this week. Separate what you saw or heard from what you concluded.
steps: Describe only what a camera would have recorded.
Describe what you concluded from it.
Name one other conclusion that fits the same facts.

title: The word 'always'
prompt: Find a thought of yours that contains words like always, never, everyone or nobody. Check how far it really reaches.
steps: Write the thought as you first phrased it.
Look for one occasion where it did not hold.
Rewrite the thought so that it is accurate.
Notice whether the rewritten version changes what you want to do.

title: Through someone else's eyes
prompt: Choose a recent conversation or situation with another person. Retell it from their point of view.
steps: Describe the situation in two sentences from your own view.
Retell it as the other person might: what did they want, what did they worry about?
Note one thing you had not considered before.
Decide whether anything in your next step would change.

title: The observer in the room
prompt: Imagine a calm, fair observer who watched a recent disagreement or tense moment from the corner of the room.
steps: Write what the observer saw happening, without taking sides.
Write what the observer would say each person needed.
Compare this with your own account: where do they differ?

title: A year from now
prompt: Take something that feels large today. Look at it from the viewpoint of yourself one year from now.
steps: Describe today's situation in a few sentences.
Write a short note about it as you a year later, who has seen how it turned out.
Write what that later self would like you to do or not do today.

title: Two other readings
prompt: Pick an event that you interpreted in a negative way. Find two other readings that fit the same facts.
steps: Write the event and your first interpretation.
Write a second interpretation that is neutral.
Write a third interpretation that is more generous.
Note which reading you would check first, and how.

title: What else could this be?
prompt: Think of a setback from the past weeks. Ask what else it could be, besides a failure.
steps: Describe the setback in plain words.
List two things it might have given you or shown you.
Write one sentence about it that you can accept as true.

title: Same story, other headline
prompt: Take a day or situation you remember as difficult. Write two different headlines for it.
steps: Write the headline you would give it today.
Write a second headline that stresses something different.
Write two or three sentences under the second headline.
Note what changes when you read that version.

title: Options and criteria
prompt: Choose a decision that is still open. Lay out the options and what matters for choosing between them.
steps: Write the decision as a question.
List at least two options, including 'do nothing'.
List the three criteria that matter most to you.
For each option, note briefly how it fares on each criterion.
Write which option looks best now and what would change your mind.

title: A look ahead at what could go wrong
prompt: Take a plan you intend to carry out. Imagine it is half a year later and it did not work out. Why?
steps: Write the plan in one sentence.
List three plausible reasons it did not work out.
For the most likely one, write what you could do now to lessen it.
Write whether the plan still looks right to you.

title: What do I still need to know?
prompt: Think of a decision you are circling around. Find out which missing piece of information would help most.
steps: Write what you know for sure about the decision.
Write what you only guess.
Pick the one guess that matters most and note how you could find out more about it.

title: And then what?
prompt: Pick a choice you made or are about to make. Follow its consequences a few steps further than usual.
steps: Write the choice.
Write what will most likely happen next.
Write what happens as a result of that.
Write what happens after that, in a month or a year.
Note whether anything on the path surprises you.

title: Who else is affected?
prompt: Take a habit or a decision of yours. Look at the effects on other people and on your future days.
steps: Write the habit or decision.
List the direct effects you notice right away.
List the later effects, on others and on you.
Write one change that would keep the good effects and reduce the unwanted ones.

title: The short and the long run
prompt: Choose something you did to make a situation easier right now. Compare the short and the long effect.
steps: Write what you did and why it helped at the time.
Write what it may cost or cause later.
Decide whether you would do the same again.

title: Only the evidence I like
prompt: Think of an opinion you hold firmly. Check which kind of evidence you notice and which you skip.
steps: Write the opinion in one sentence.
List what supports it.
Actively look for what speaks against it and list it.
Write whether the two lists are equally easy to fill, and what that tells you.

title: A judgement made quickly
prompt: Pick a quick judgement you made about a person or a situation. Look for a thinking habit that may have shaped it.
steps: Describe the judgement and what it was based on.
Ask: did I rely on a first impression, on one example, or on what I expected to see?
Name one fact you would want before judging the same way again.

title: Looking back, it was obvious
prompt: Recall an outcome you now feel you 'knew all along'. Check what you actually knew at the time.
steps: Write what happened.
Write what you really knew and expected before it happened.
Note what looks obvious only now.

title: Explain it to a friend
prompt: Choose something you learned lately. Explain it in plain words, as you would to a friend who knows nothing about it.
steps: Write the topic and the main idea in one or two sentences.
Explain it with everyday words and no jargon.
Add one example from daily life.
Mark the places where your explanation was vague, and note what you would look up.

title: Three sentences
prompt: Pick an idea you want to understand better. Say it in three sentences.
steps: Write what the idea is.
Write why it matters or how it works.
Write what it is often confused with.
Read it back and shorten wherever you can.

title: Find the gaps
prompt: Take a topic you believe you know well. Explain it step by step and see where the explanation gets thin.
steps: Write the topic.
Explain it from the beginning, step by step, without looking anything up.
Underline each step where you hesitated.
Write one question for each gap.
